description: I’m an AI engineer interested in space exploration and autonomous robotics. With RedBot, I’m building a game where players design a Mars rover mission, choose its scientific instruments, and watch it navigate Martian terrain on its own. The game draws on NASA’s open resources to show how choices about payload, power, and communications affect what the rover can discover and send back to Earth.
summary: RedBot is a 3D browser game that lets learners design, test, and operate a robotic Mars surface mission. Players build a six-wheel rover, quadruped, or humanoid biped, test it indoors, deploy it on Mars, collect science, and relay results to Earth. NASA/JPL’s Perseverance traverse and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery, together with USGS elevation data, connect the game to real sites in Jezero Crater. Limited mass, battery power, and relay opportunities make each design choice matter. Players can replay their missions and compare results to see how one engineering decision changes what their robot can accomplish.
details:
What players do

RedBot is a 3D browser game about designing a Mars surface mission. Players build a six-wheel rover, quadruped, or humanoid biped, configure its hardware and navigation, and test it indoors. The same robot then lands on Mars and carries out one of three simulated science tasks: panoramic imaging, spectral comparison, or core sampling. Driving and science run automatically by default, and players can take over driving.

An engineering decision that changes the mission

The build room lets players see the consequences of each change before they fly. In the core sampling rehearsal, upgrading the starter rover’s radio adds 2 kg, bringing launch mass to 33 kg against a 34 kg limit. The game forecasts that the three science records can then be sent in one orbital pass instead of two. The player can compare that forecast with the mission debrief.

Real Mars data

NASA/JPL’s Perseverance traverse and waypoints anchor the training routes in Jezero Crater. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery provides map context, and USGS elevation data supplies slopes for route planning and energy estimates. The robots, lander, local hazards, relay timing, and science readings are simulated.

Learning value

RedBot lets learners change one part at a time and compare the results. They can see how terrain, mass, battery power, and communication windows affect what a robot can accomplish. After the primary relay, players can end the mission or use their remaining resources for bonus surveys. Replays and scores are saved in the browser for comparison.

Tools and implementation

RedBot uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js/WebGL. Python, NumPy, and Rasterio were used to prepare the orbital data. The interface is available in English and Japanese, with detailed navigation settings for players who want to experiment further.
